source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy, Cognitive Science 7
finding: States the systematicity principle as the third of three mapping rules: drop object attributes, keep relations between objects, and among relations keep the ones that belong to a connected system governed by higher-order relations.
numbers: Rules: (1) discard attributes, (2) preserve relations, (3) systematicity. Order of a relation = 1 + max order of its arguments; first-order takes objects, CAUSE over relations is second-order.
quote: To decide which relations are preserved, choose systems of relations
limits: It is a theory at the level of syntax: no domain content is used. Only the Rutherford and heat-water cases are shown as demonstrations.
agent_relevance: Gives a content-free scoring rule for O7: score a mapping by how deeply its matched relations are connected, not by how many items match.

source: Gentner (1983) - Rutherford and heat/water demonstrations of systematicity
finding: Why MORE MASSIVE THAN (sun, planet) maps to the atom but HOTTER THAN does not: only the first sits inside the central-force system of connected predicates. Dynamic causal chains are usually more deeply embedded than static facts, so a purely structural rule favours causal knowledge without a content rule.
numbers: Heat/water example: chain 2 (puncture causes water to flow out) is preferred over chain 1 (vessel has a lid) because it is embedded in a CAUSE.
limits: Assumes the hearer already knows the object correspondences; Gentner notes the order of processing is really variable. Partial knowledge of the system is assumed enough to gauge its connectedness.
agent_relevance: Depth of embedding is a cheap proxy for inferential value. Our agent can prefer a source step that sits under a cause or goal relation over an isolated fact.

source: Gentner (1983) - empirical support cited in the paper
finding: Subjects wrote interpretations of analogies such as 'a cigarette is like a time bomb'. Judges coded each statement as attribute or relation. Interpretations of analogies were mostly relational; descriptions of the same objects were not. Aptness ratings correlated with the amount of relational content.
numbers: No sample sizes or coefficients are given in this paper; it points to Gentner (1980b) for the full study.
limits: The 1983 paper has no direct test of systematicity. The first direct tests are Gentner and Toupin (1986) and Clement and Gentner (1991).
agent_relevance: Do not cite the 1983 paper as evidence for systematicity itself. It is the proposal, not the proof.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping, Cognitive Science 15:89-132 - Experiment 1
finding: Subjects read a base and target passage and judged which of two matching facts mattered more to the analogy: one embedded in a shared causal system, one isolated. Analogy subjects preferred the shared-system fact. A target-only control group, who never saw the base, did not.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates (analogy and target-only groups; 4 passages). Rating 1-9: shared-system M=6.28 vs different-system M=4.89 for analogy group; target-only M=5.22 vs 5.31. Condition x fact-type F'(1,44)=13.99, p<.001; simple effect in analogy group F'(1,11)=10.44, p<.01. Choice score (0-4): analogy 3.17 vs target-only 2.0, F(1,44)=18.43, p<.001. Per passage analogy chose shared-system fact 67% to 92%; target-only 42% to 54%; significant on 3 of 4 passages (Fisher, one-tailed p<.05).
limits: Short written stories with the passages available. Items were made so both key facts were plausible. Only 3 of 4 passages reached significance in the choice task.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a connected-system match is judged more relevant than an equally good isolated match. The control without the base rules out plain salience.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) - Experiment 1 justifications
finding: When subjects picked the shared-system fact they often named the causal link behind it. When they rejected a fact they often said it was not connected to the common structure. Subjects did not always give higher-order reasons, so awareness was partial.
numbers: Out of 96 choice opportunities, justifications were coded by two judges into four categories (higher-order link, lower-order similarity of the fact, the fact alone, other).
limits: Self-report; the authors say subjects often could not articulate the higher-order connection.
agent_relevance: The preference may run without explicit reasons. A scored mapping should not need the model to verbalise why a system is central.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) - Experiment 2: analogical predictions
finding: Subjects were asked to predict new facts about the target. They predicted the fact that followed from the causal system shared with the base far more than an equally plausible fact that would have matched an isolated base fact.
numbers: N=32 undergraduates, 16 per group, 4 analogies. Analogy group: .53 of responses predicted the shared-system fact and .12 the different-system fact; target-only group: .12 and .12 (rest other). About .08 of responses named both and were dropped. Interrater agreement .88.
limits: Passages were available during the task. Both predictions were possible given the target text.
agent_relevance: Candidate inferences are chosen by connection to the matched system. Rank candidate inferences by the support they get from higher-order relations.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) - Experiment 3: memory only, and the failed passage
finding: Repeated Experiment 2 with the base passage no longer on view, so subjects mapped from memory. The systematicity effect held overall but was weaker, and one passage failed.
numbers: N=24 per group. Mean (shared-system minus different-system predictions over 3 passages): analogy .92 vs target-only .13, F(1,44)=5.15, p<.05. Passage 2: analogy subjects predicted each fact type equally often (.375 each). Choice task: shared-system chosen 87% and 69% vs target-only 44% and 25% on two passages (p<.05); on the other two passages 62% and 75% vs 69% and 44%, not different.
limits: The authors blame poor memory for the base on the failed passage; this is an explanation, not a test. Two of four passages in the choice task did not separate the groups.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the effect depends on the base causal structure being accurately held. A weak or wrong source representation removes the benefit.

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy, Cognitive Science 10:277-300 - design
finding: Children acted out a target story using a base story they had just heard. The base was either systematic (a moral gives a higher-order causal structure) or nonsystematic (same events, no moral). Mapping difficulty varied by whether similar characters played the same roles (S/S), different roles (S/D, cross-mapped) or were new (D).
numbers: N=72 children: 36 aged 4-6 and 36 aged 8-10, systematicity between subjects; 3 mapping conditions within. Systematic stories averaged about 200 words vs about 170 for nonsystematic.
limits: The systematic stories were longer and added a moral, so some length confound remains; the authors argue the effect is specific to hard mappings, not general.
agent_relevance: The classic demonstration that higher-order structure helps keep lower-order roles straight under confusing object matches.

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) - results
finding: Systematicity helped only the older children and only in the hardest, cross-mapped condition. Everyone did nearly perfectly on the easy mapping, so the effect is not just better memory of systematic stories.
numbers: ANOVA Age x Systematicity x Mapping: Age F(1,68)=14.93, p<.001; Systematicity F(1,68)=6.28, p<.05; Mapping F(2,136)=29.01, p<.000001; Systematicity x Mapping F(2,136)=3.89, p<.05. Older group: systematic better, t(34)=2.48, p<.01; younger group: t(34)=1.08, n.s. Effect significant only in the S/D condition.
limits: A footnote indicates no significant Age x Systematicity interaction, so the claim that younger children cannot use systematicity rests on a difference between simple effects. Informal self-corrections by older children are anecdotal.
agent_relevance: Systematic structure acts as an error checker on local role assignments. In our agent a higher-order constraint can be used to detect and repair a wrong role binding.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity, American Psychologist 52:45-56
finding: States systematicity as a defining trait of analogy: matching sets of relations tied together by higher-order constraining relations make a better match than an equal number of unconnected matching relations. Links it to a preference for coherence and causal predictive power.
numbers: Review; cites Clement and Gentner (1991), Forbus and Gentner (1989), Gentner (1983). Picture example: one pair of scenes aligns on 'child looks at pet', another on 'animal frightened by animal'; the shared connected system is what comparison highlights.
quote: We are not much interested in analogies that capture a series of coincidences
limits: A review, so no new data here.
agent_relevance: Frames the scoring goal: reward coherent systems, not counts of coincidences.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) - asymmetry, transfer and retrieval dissociation
finding: Asymmetry of comparison arises when one item is more systematic than the other: the more systematic item is preferred as base because more can be projected. Retrieval is driven by surface (object) overlap while soundness and similarity ratings are driven by shared higher-order structure.
numbers: Reports: the more shared objects and characters, the more likely a story was retrieved; the more shared higher-order causal structure, the higher the rated soundness. People often rated their own remindings low in soundness. Systematic higher-order structure can allow transfer even under adverse object matches.
limits: Secondary report of Bowdle and Gentner (1996) and Gentner, Rattermann and Forbus (1993); I did not open those papers.
agent_relevance: Retrieval and scoring should use different signals. Retrieve cheaply on surface, then score the mapping structurally (the MAC/FAC split).

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus and Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples, Artificial Intelligence 41 - trickle-down rule
finding: SME implements systematicity locally: a match hypothesis passes 80% of its belief to the match hypotheses of its arguments (trickle-down). A deep matched system therefore gives the object matches under it high scores. The gmap score (SES) is the sum of evidence for its match hypotheses.
numbers: Rule: (implies (MH b1 t1) (MH b2 t2) (0.8 . 0.0)). Same-functor evidence 0.5 per match. Dempster's rule for combining gmap evidence was replaced by plain summation because of roundoff with many match hypotheses and because normalising gmap evidence blocks comparison across different bases.
quote: The more matched structure that exists above a given match hypothesis, the more that hypothesis will be believed
limits: The sum is not normalised for size of base and target (the authors say so). Other structural factors, such as the number and size of structural discontinuities, are listed as missing.
agent_relevance: A concrete, programmable scoring rule for a mapping: sum local match scores with a downward cascade. We can implement it in about 30 lines in code, which fits guardrail G5 (code selects).

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus and Gentner (1989) - Rutherford atom worked example
finding: SME built three interpretations of the solar system to atom analogy. The standard one, driven by the mass inequality inside the attraction system, scored highest. A reading that mapped temperature difference to mass difference scored lower because no systematic structure hung on temperature. A spurious reading scored lowest.
numbers: SES: 6.03 (standard), 4.04 (temperature to mass), 1.87 (sun mass to electron mass, nucleus mass to planet). Two reasons for 4.04: different functions get less local evidence, and no mappable systematic structure around temperature.
limits: Hand-coded, simplified representations. The authors say a home-heating target would reverse the outcome, because the structure comes from the target as well.
agent_relevance: The preferred mapping by score is also the one that supports the most inferences. Use the score to rank competing readings, not as a truth test.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus and Gentner (1989) - Karla story simulation of human soundness and access data
finding: SME was run on five story triads from a human study. With analogy rules the cross-domain analogy outscored the surface-matched story; with mere-appearance rules the order flipped. This matches human soundness ratings (analogy high) and human retrieval (appearance high).
numbers: Analogy rules: 'Zerdia the country' SES=22.4 vs 'Zerdia the eagle' SES=16.8. Appearance rules: eagle story 7.7 vs country story 6.4. Story set 5 is shown in detail; the paper says SME's rankings agree over the five sets.
limits: Only ordinal agreement over five hand-encoded stories. No statistics and no independent coders for the representations.
agent_relevance: The same engine can give a structure score and a surface score. Our agent could track both and flag cases where they disagree.

source: Forbus and Gentner (1989) Structural evaluation of analogies: what counts? CogSci 11 - sensitivity analysis of the scoring rule
finding: Tests how the systematicity preference should be implemented. They reduce SME's structural evaluation from 8 parameters to 3 (Same-Predicate, Same-Function, Trickle-Down), and sweep them against human soundness data (analogy rated more sound than mere appearance).
numbers: 343 parameter points (7^3) per algorithm; 6,174 evaluations for three story sets. Working region for trickle-down with additive-max normalisation: Same-Predicate in [0.001, 0.01], Same-Function in [0.0001, 0.01], Trickle-Down in [4, 16], all fit perfectly. Failing: Trickle-Down 1.0 or less, Same-Predicate 0.3 or more, Same-Function 0.9 or more. Cutting 8 parameters to 3 took about two Symbolics-days of sensitivity analysis.
limits: Fit is binary (does the analogy beat the appearance match in 3 triads), not a correlation with human ratings. The table percentages were lost in text extraction, so only the stated regions are recorded.
agent_relevance: The score is robust over a sizeable parameter region, but needs a strong downward cascade. A weak cascade lets surface matches swamp structure.

source: Forbus and Gentner (1989) - Specificity Conjecture and swamping
finding: Claims human memory representations are mostly bottom-heavy (much appearance and low-order information, little higher-order structure). In such descriptions surface matches outnumber structural matches, so a scoring rule must resist being swamped. Dempster-Shafer combination swamps and fits the human data only for top-heavy descriptions; additive-max with trickle-down fits all three representation types.
numbers: Bottom-heavy set built with twice as many match hypotheses for the appearance match as for the analogy match. A footnote notes people retrieved appearance matches better than analogies, which implies they stored many low-order facts.
quote: People apparently have the ability to find structural commonalities even when they have bottom-heavy representations
limits: The conjecture is argued, not measured: the paper says there is very little direct evidence about how top-heavy human representations are.
agent_relevance: LLM-written source and target descriptions are likely bottom-heavy (much surface detail). A scorer needs a cascade or a restriction to relational facts, or it will favour lexical overlap.

source: Forbus and Gentner (1989) - trickle-down versus order-scoring
finding: Two ways to implement systematicity: pass scores down to arguments (trickle-down, signals connectivity) or scale each match by its relation order (order-scoring, signals only that higher-order relations exist). Only trickle-down survived the bottom-heavy test.
numbers: Order formula tested: O3(MH)=Min(1.0, C x [1 + Order(MH) x Order-Bias]) with Order-Bias in {0,0.5,1,2,4,8,16}. It fails on bottom-heavy sets because local normalisation caps each match. They also predict an 'order cutoff': past some depth, extra systematicity cannot be told apart.
limits: Computed on the authors' own encoded triads; no independent human data for the cutoff prediction.
agent_relevance: A count of higher-order relations alone is a weak signal. Connectivity (what is tied to what) is the thing to score.

source: Lassaline (1996) causal structure in category-based induction (as described by Colhoun and Gentner 2009 and Lee and Holyoak 2007)
finding: Reported by others: more shared causal relations make the inference stronger; a causal relation supports a stronger inference than a non-causal 'temporally prior to' relation; when the cause is shared, people infer the effect.
numbers: No numbers are given in the two papers I read. Lee and Holyoak say both similarity and inductive strength rose with added shared properties.
limits: Not opened. Rehder (2006) is noted by Lee and Holyoak as confounded: the single causal relation was also the only higher-order relation.
agent_relevance: Causal relations are the usual carrier of higher-order structure. In practice 'higher-order' and 'causal' are nearly the same thing, which the 1983 syntax-only claim does not say.

source: Lee and Holyoak (2007) Causal models guide analogical inference, CogSci 29 - Experiment 1
finding: Challenge to systematicity: removing a matching preventive cause from the target lowered similarity but raised inductive strength. The better-matching argument gave a weaker inference.
numbers: N=42 undergraduates (half similarity, half inductive strength), 9 arguments. Similarity ratings N1N2P=7.58, N1N2=4.77, N1P=5.09 (main effect F(2,36)=16.79, p<.001). Inductive strength (0-100) N1N2P=33.60, N1N2=58.57, N1P=35.32.
limits: Some participants objected that the 'prevents' wording implied certainty; Experiment 2 added 'tends to'. Artificial animal descriptions with letter-coded features.
agent_relevance: Matching more relations is not always better. A preventer in the source that is also in the target lowers the odds of the effect. A mapping score alone is not a probability that the transferred step holds.

source: Lee and Holyoak (2007) - Experiment 2 with probabilistic wording
finding: With causes made probabilistic ('tends to'), the dissociation held: with only generative causes, three shared causes beat two on both measures; with a preventer added, similarity rose but inductive strength fell.
numbers: N=60 UCLA undergraduates (30 per measure). Similarity G1G2G3 vs G1G2 differed t(29)=4.44, p<.001, an increase of 1.55 points (8.17 for G1G2G3). In the generative+preventive set, G1G2P had higher similarity than G1G2 but lower inductive strength.
limits: This is a conference version; the 2008 JEP:LMC article was not opened. The authors argue all extant models using copy-with-substitution-and-generation predict the opposite order.
agent_relevance: Supports a division of labour for the agent: structure scoring picks the correspondence, then a separate step estimates whether the inferred step will hold.

source: Colhoun and Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies - Study 1 replication and similarity versus effect inference
finding: Replicated the Lee and Holyoak dissociation for the single effect inference (similarity GGP > GG > GP, effect inference GG > GGP > GP). But when all candidate inferences were rated, inductive strength matched the similarity ordering, as structure mapping predicts.
numbers: Study 1A N=70 Northwestern undergraduates (36 similarity, 34 inference). Similarity: GGP M=7.53 (SD 1.72), GG M=6.35 (SD 1.99), GP M=5.01 (SD 1.34), F(2,286)=44.4, p<.0001. Proportion endorsing the effect inference about .86, .65 and .18 in Figure 3b.
limits: Conference paper. The mapping of the three proportions to target types is read from the text, as figure labels did not extract cleanly. The effect inference was only one of several candidate inferences.
agent_relevance: The apparent clash between similarity and inductive strength is mostly a clash over which inference is asked about. Score the whole set of candidate inferences, not one.

source: Colhoun and Gentner (2009) - Study 2 and SME simulation
finding: Effect ratings differed only when the effect E was shown in the base; they did not depend on whether the causal relations were stated in the base or the target, or whether an analogy was done at all. So the base supplies a causal model and a rough posterior, and the effect check can be a later step. A simulation using SME followed by a simple post-mapping calculation reproduced the human pattern.
numbers: Study 2: Group x Target-type F(6,76)=2.8, p<.05; Group F(3,76)=4.4, p<.01; Target type F=83.5, p<.0001 (as printed). Only the Analogy-BaseRelations+E group differed. Simulation took the highest-SES mapping and used candidate-inference support scores.
limits: The simulation is a proof of concept on stimuli with blank features. Fit to human data is described as very close but no correlation is reported in the text.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema's separation: structure mapping proposes, a causal check disposes (guardrails G2 and G3).

source: Myers and Gentner (2017) Analogical inferences in causal systems, CogSci 39
finding: Tested whether the base-target dissociation comes from an inferred higher-order relation of relative strength (generative cause stronger than the sum of preventers). A target matching a base with one generative and two preventive causes got higher effect inference than a target matching more first-order relations, with similarity not different.
numbers: N=40 Northwestern students, 32 analysed. Effect inference G1P1P2 M=62.28 (SD 19.84) vs G1G2P1 M=47.28 (SD 17.49), t(31)=3.44, p<.005. Similarity 6.25 vs 5.78, t(31)=1.54, p=.13. Experiment 2 (same participants): Familiar P M=62.31 vs Novel P M=48.59, t(31)=3.71, p<.001; similarity 6.44 vs 4.19, t(31)=6.95.
limits: Same participants in both experiments; 8 of 40 excluded. The higher-order relation is inferred, not shown to the subject.
agent_relevance: Higher-order relations can be built while encoding the source and then carried over. A good source summary for the agent should state relative strength of causes, not only the list.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) ACME, as discussed by Forbus and Gentner (1989) and Lee and Holyoak (2007)
finding: Competing constraint-satisfaction model. Forbus and Gentner say it overlaps heavily with SME at the information and algorithm levels, so SME could run in a localist connectionist net. They note ACME needs a numerical similarity score for each predicate pair, so its parameter count is at least the square of the number of predicates. Lee and Holyoak group ACME and LISA with SME as 'copy with substitution and generation' models.
numbers: No numbers from ACME itself; I did not open the ACME paper.
limits: Secondary account, partly from a rival camp. Not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Systematicity can be an emergent effect of parallel constraint satisfaction as well as an explicit rule. Either way the scoring principle is similar.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives - framework
finding: Builds a narrative benchmark from Gentner's surface mappings (entities, attributes, surface relations) versus system mappings (interconnected relational correspondences, here via shared proverbs). Far analogies have system mappings with no surface overlap; near analogies have both. Distractors are far or near disanalogies.
numbers: Four partitions of far/near analogy facing far/near distractor. Human testing on about 10% of the dataset (30 items).
limits: System mapping is approximated by a shared proverb, a coarse stand-in for a connected relational system. The human sample is small.
agent_relevance: Gives a test set that isolates relational-system matching from surface matching. We could use its far/near split to check our own mapping scorer.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN - results for humans and LLMs
finding: LLMs do about as well as people on near analogies but fail on far analogies, which are exactly the ones needing system mapping. GPT-4 was near human on near analogies but below random on far analogies.
numbers: Overall humans 96% vs models 57%. Near analogies: humans 97.9% vs models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1% vs models 39.6% average (below the 50% random baseline). Human accuracy by partition 98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4 (mean 96.0).
limits: Models tested (GPT-3.5 up to GPT-4) are 2023 models; later models may differ. Binary choice with one analogy and one distractor.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that an LLM left alone prefers surface overlap over relational system match. A scaffold that scores system match in code should help most on far analogies.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models - story analogies
finding: Re-ran the 18 'far analogy' story problems with Gentner-style causal structure (correct story shares causal structure but not surface; incorrect story shares surface events but not causal structure). GPT-4 showed an answer-order bias and fell when the correct story was paraphrased to remove sentence-level similarity.
numbers: Earlier study (Webb et al.) GPT-4: 0.89 (16/18) when correct answer first, 0.61 (11/18) second, 0.75 overall. This study GPT-4 (0613): 1.0 first, 0.72 second, 0.86 (31/36) overall on originals, 0.72 (26/36) on paraphrased correct stories. Humans (245 Prolific participants, 6 problems each, 720 responses): 0.78 (564/720) on originals, 0.70 (503/720) on paraphrased. Humans showed no order bias.
limits: Only 18 problems, so the authors say the GPT-4 versus human drop on paraphrase is hard to call significant. Table text in the extracted PDF was misaligned; the row-to-model mapping was read with care but not checked against the figure. The stories may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Part of the apparent success on structure-based story analogies may be sentence-level similarity. Our test sets need paraphrased and order-swapped controls.

source: Sultan and Shahaf (2022) Life is a circus and we are the clowns: automatically finding analogies between situations and processes - objective function
finding: A pipeline built on structure-mapping theory extracts entities and verb relations with QA-SRL and finds a one-to-one mapping. Its objective sums the relational similarity of every pair of mapped entities. It has no term for higher-order relations or system depth, so it scores pairwise relational agreement, not systematicity.
numbers: Objective: maximise the sum over base entity pairs of sim(R(bi,bj), R(M(bi),M(bj))); relations are verbs or QA-SRL questions; mapping into 'empty' scores 0.
limits: A pairwise sum is a coarse proxy for a connected system. The authors say their goal is a reasonable model, not the best one.
agent_relevance: A cheap approximation to systematicity: agreement over entity pairs rewards consistent role mappings. Adding higher-order links (cause, goal) would strengthen it.

source: Sultan and Shahaf (2022) - results
finding: The method found far and sub-analogies that a sentence-embedding baseline missed, and produced mappings that agree with human annotators.
numbers: Mapping precision top-3: 0.87 on ProPara process texts, 0.94 on cognitive-psychology stories (Rattermann and Keane problems); the question-based version beat the verb-only version on all metrics. Mining 76K paragraph pairs: precision at top 100 was 79% (question-based) vs 72% (verb-only); SBERT reached 100% but mostly found self-analogies. Analogy prevalence about 3%. Annotators agreed with the expert 0.96 (binary) and 0.73 (5-class); Fleiss kappa 0.82 and 0.58.
limits: Stories were written as analogies with explicit parallels, which the authors say explains the higher score. Mapping evaluation used 15 pairs chosen from the mining step, a possible bias they acknowledge.
agent_relevance: Structure-based mapping can be done by code from extracted relations. It works best when the two texts are written with parallel structure.

source: Gentner, Rattermann and Forbus (1993) Roles of similarity in transfer (as reported in Gentner and Markman 1997 and Myers and Gentner 2017)
finding: Reported by others: deeply embedded relational structures were perceived as more similar than shallow ones; the overlap that drove retrieval (objects) differed from the overlap that drove soundness (shared causal structure).
numbers: No numbers in the secondary reports. See the sibling subfield (structure mapping) for the primary study.
limits: Not opened by me; relies on secondary description.
agent_relevance: Same dissociation as in the Karla story simulation: retrieve on surface, evaluate on structure.

source: Boundary summary for systematicity (from the papers opened)
finding: Systematicity is supported when subjects must pick which match counts (Clement and Gentner 1991) and when role confusion makes mapping hard (Gentner and Toupin 1986, only in the hardest condition and only for older children). It is challenged for the effect inference when a preventer is shared (Lee and Holyoak 2007), but the challenge shrinks when all candidate inferences are asked (Colhoun and Gentner 2009) and when a relative-strength relation is encoded (Myers and Gentner 2017). Gentner's 1983 claim that the rule ignores content sits oddly with the fact that nearly all higher-order examples are causal.
numbers: Synthesis of the lines above; sample sizes range from N=24 to N=72 per group or study.
limits: This line is my synthesis of sources I opened, not a published meta-analysis. No meta-analysis of systematicity was found. Web search quota ran out, so forward citation tracing is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Use systematicity to rank competing mappings and candidate inferences, never as proof the transferred step is true. Pair it with a held-out check (guardrail G3).
